steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Ruledger, a ledger-based platform that protects the integrity of rule executions in trigger-action IoT / smart home systems. Explain the setting and the threat, why existing defenses fall short, what Ruledger does and how it performs, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Smart home / IoT devices and trigger-action platforms
2. Security threats, especially violation of rule execution integrity
3. Existing approaches and why they fall short
4. Ruledger: idea, mechanism, prototype and overhead
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Setting
- smart home systems and IoT devices proliferating
- devices: Samsung SmartThings smart lock, Garmin smart watch, bulbs, smoke detectors
- managed via trigger-action platforms: IFTTT, Microsoft Flow, Zapier
- users set up rules -> automated rule executions; platforms manage devices from different vendors, perform physical or virtual tasks

2. Threats
- privacy leakage; violation of rule execution integrity (major concern)
- example: fake location sent to IFTTT -> rule opens smart lock while nobody is home
- leaked OAuth tokens / compromised part of system -> access user locations, remotely control devices via APIs

3. Existing work
- extensively studied, but none effectively protects rule execution integrity (Table I)
- ESO: situational access control by encapsulating IoT remote APIs; cannot avoid fake triggers
- DTAP: secure token authorization only; cannot prevent malicious rule executions triggered by IoT platforms themselves
- Peeves: only prevents event spoofing by verifying physical events
- -> still no protection for rule execution integrity

4. Ruledger
- systematic study of vulnerabilities enabling malicious rule executions
- root cause: no mechanism ensuring authenticity and integrity of messages between components
- ledger-based IoT platform, integrates with existing platforms
- three ledger wallets -> stateful records according to real information; smart contracts -> protect rule configuration, verify trigger events and action requests
- all action requests and events recorded as stateful transaction logs -> verify authenticity
- prevents faked event sources of rule triggers, malicious action requests from platforms
- security analysis: integrity under various attacks
- prototype with real IoT devices + IFTTT; delay up ~12.53%, throughput overhead down ~6.5% vs baseline; acceptable for real deployment

5. Contributions
- systematic study of vulnerabilities
- Ruledger platform verifying events and execution states
- state generation and verification algorithms on ledgers and wallets
- prototype + experiments with real-world IoT platforms

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently there has been a proliferation of smart home systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Users have many different devices in their smart home systems, e.g. the smart lock of Samsung SmartThings, the smart watch of Garmin, and also bulbs and smoke detectors. All of these can be managed through trigger-action platforms like IFTTT, Microsoft Flow and Zapier, and they work together to provide different functionalities. Users set up rules in these trigger-action platforms so that the rule executions in their devices are automated. In this way the platforms are able to manage many devices from different vendors and to perform physical or virtual tasks automatically based on the rules.

But smart home systems also face severe security threats, like privacy leakage and violation of rule execution integrity. Violating rule execution integrity in particular has become a major concern for smart home security. For example, an attacker can send a fake location to the trigger-action platform, e.g. IFTTT, and then the platform triggers the rule that opens the smart lock even when nobody is at home. In the same way, if the OAuth tokens in the smart home system are leaked or part of the system is compromised, an attacker can easily get user locations and control IoT devices remotely by invoking APIs.

The security risks of smart home systems have been studied a lot in the literature. But as Table I shows, none of the existing approaches can effectively protect the integrity of rule executions in these systems. ESO, for example, enforces situational access control for trigger-action platforms by encapsulating IoT remote APIs, but this cannot avoid fake triggers in the trigger-action platforms. DTAP only enables secure token authorization for trigger-action platforms, and it cannot prevent malicious rule executions that are triggered by the IoT platforms themselves. Peeves also can only prevent event spoofing attacks, by verifying physical events in IoT devices. So current trigger-action based smart home systems still do not have protection for the integrity of rule execution.

- Ruledger: systematic study of vulnerabilities enabling malicious rule executions; root cause = no mechanism for authenticity/integrity of messages between components
- ledger-based IoT platform, integrates with existing platforms; three ledger wallets + smart contracts; all action requests and events as stateful transaction logs
- prevents faked event sources and malicious action requests; security analysis under various attacks
- prototype with real IoT devices + IFTTT; delay ~12.53% more, throughput overhead ~6.5% less vs baseline; acceptable

- contributions: vulnerability study; Ruledger; state generation and verification algorithms; prototype + experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently there has been a proliferation of smart home systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Users have many different devices in their smart home systems, e.g. the smart lock of Samsung SmartThings, the smart watch of Garmin, and also bulbs and smoke detectors. All of these can be managed through trigger-action platforms like IFTTT, Microsoft Flow and Zapier, and they work together to provide different functionalities. Users set up rules in these trigger-action platforms so that the rule executions in their devices are automated. In this way the platforms are able to manage many devices from different vendors and to perform physical or virtual tasks automatically based on the rules.

But smart home systems also face severe security threats, like privacy leakage and violation of rule execution integrity. Violating rule execution integrity in particular has become a major concern for smart home security. For example, an attacker can send a fake location to the trigger-action platform, e.g. IFTTT, and then the platform triggers the rule that opens the smart lock even when nobody is at home. In the same way, if the OAuth tokens in the smart home system are leaked or part of the system is compromised, an attacker can easily get user locations and control IoT devices remotely by invoking APIs.

The security risks of smart home systems have been studied a lot in the literature. But as Table I shows, none of the existing approaches can effectively protect the integrity of rule executions in these systems. ESO, for example, enforces situational access control for trigger-action platforms by encapsulating IoT remote APIs, but this cannot avoid fake triggers in the trigger-action platforms. DTAP only enables secure token authorization for trigger-action platforms, and it cannot prevent malicious rule executions that are triggered by the IoT platforms themselves. Peeves also can only prevent event spoofing attacks, by verifying physical events in IoT devices. So current trigger-action based smart home systems still do not have protection for the integrity of rule execution.

In this paper we study systematically the vulnerabilities that make malicious rule executions possible in smart home systems. The root cause of these vulnerabilities is that there is no mechanism to ensure the authenticity and integrity of the messages that are transferred between the different components of smart home systems. So we propose Ruledger, a ledger-based IoT platform that can be integrated with existing platforms, which ensures the integrity of rule executions by making it possible to verify the information in smart home systems. Ruledger uses three ledger wallets to guarantee stateful records according to real information, and it uses smart contracts to protect rule configuration and to verify the trigger events and action requests according to the stateful ledger records. All the action requests and events are recorded in the ledger as stateful transaction logs, so Ruledger can verify the authenticity of all the information associated with rule executions based on the logs and the execution states in the ledger. This way Ruledger can effectively prevent faked event sources of rule triggers and malicious action requests coming from the trigger-action platforms. Our security analysis proves that Ruledger ensures rule execution integrity under various attacks. We build a prototype of Ruledger with real IoT devices and the mainstream trigger-action platform, which is IFTTT, and we evaluate how Ruledger performs. The experimental results show that the overhead of Ruledger is acceptable for real deployment. Compared to the baseline systems, the delay increases by about 12.53% and the throughput overhead decreases by about 6.5%.

Our contributions are the following.

- We study systematically the vulnerabilities that violate the integrity of rule executions in trigger-action based smart home systems.

- We present Ruledger, a ledger based IoT platform, that verifies the authenticity of the information (events and their execution states) and ensures that rule executions keep their integrity.

- We develop state generation and verification algorithms on top of ledgers and wallets, to guarantee that the states of the transactions in a smart home system are verified and submitted properly.

- We build a prototype of Ruledger, and experiments with real-world IoT platforms show its performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Smart Home Systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices have proliferated recently. Users use various devices in their smart home systems, e.g. the smart lock of Samsung SmartThings [1], the smart watch of Garmin, as well as bulbs and smoke detectors. All these facilities can be managed via trigger-action platforms, such as IFTTT [2], Microsoft Flow [3], and Zapier [4], and they work together to provide different functionalities. Users set up rules in these trigger-action platforms to automate rule executions in their devices. Thus, these platforms can manage various devices from different vendors and automatically perform physical or virtual tasks according to the rules.

Meanwhile, smart home systems suffer severe security threats, such as privacy leakage [5] and violation of rule execution integrity [6]. In particular, violating rule execution integrity has become a major concern of smart home security. For example, an attacker can send a fake location [7] to the trigger-action platform, e.g., IFTTT, so that the platform triggers the rule to open the smart lock even though nobody is at home. Similarly, if OAuth tokens in the smart home system are leaked or part of the system is compromised, an attacker can easily access user locations and remotely control IoT devices by invoking APIs [8,9].

These security risks have been extensively studied in the literature [9,10,7,11]. Unfortunately, as shown in Table I, none of the existing approaches can effectively protect the integrity of rule executions in smart home systems. For example, ESO [10] enforces situational access control for trigger-action platforms by encapsulating IoT remote APIs, which cannot avoid fake triggers in trigger-action platforms. DTAP [9] only enables secure token authorization for trigger-action platforms but cannot prevent malicious rule executions triggered by the IoT platforms themselves. Similarly, Peeves [7] can only prevent event spoofing attacks by verifying physical events in IoT devices. Thus, current trigger-action based smart home systems still lack protection for the integrity of rule execution.

In this paper, we systematically study the vulnerabilities that enable malicious rule executions in smart home systems. Their root cause is that no mechanism exists to ensure the authenticity and integrity of the messages transferred among the different components of smart home systems. To this end, we propose Ruledger, a ledger-based IoT platform that can be integrated with existing platforms, to ensure the integrity of rule executions by enabling verification of the information in smart home systems. In particular, Ruledger utilizes three ledger wallets to guarantee stateful records according to real information, and leverages smart contracts to protect rule configuration and to verify trigger events and action requests according to the stateful ledger records. Ruledger records all action requests and events in the ledger as stateful transaction logs, so that it can verify the authenticity of all information associated with rule executions based on the logs and the execution states in the ledger. Therefore, Ruledger can effectively prevent faked event sources of rule triggers as well as malicious action requests generated from the trigger-action platforms. Our security analysis proves that Ruledger ensures rule execution integrity under various attacks. We prototype Ruledger with real IoT devices and the mainstream trigger-action platform, i.e., IFTTT, and evaluate its performance. The experimental results show that the overhead incurred by Ruledger is acceptable for real deployment: compared to the baseline systems, the delay increases by about 12.53%, and the throughput overhead decreases by about 6.5%.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows.

- We systematically study the vulnerabilities that violate the integrity of rule executions in trigger-action based smart home systems.

- We present Ruledger, a ledger based IoT platform, which verifies the authenticity of the information (events and their corresponding execution states) and ensures the integrity of rule executions.

- We develop state generation and verification algorithms built upon ledgers and wallets to guarantee that the transaction states in a smart home system are properly verified and submitted.

- We prototype Ruledger, and experiments with real-world IoT platforms demonstrate its performance.

References:

[2] IFTTT. https://ifttt.com/ .
[3] Microsoft Flow. https://flow.microsoft.com/en-us/ .
[4] Zapier. https://zapier.com/ .
[5] L. Bauer A. Das M. Surbatovich, J. Aljuraidan and L. Jia. Some recipes can do more than spoil your appetite: Analyzing the security and privacy risks of ifttt recipes. In WWW , page 1501–1510, 2017.
[6] M. Balliu I. Bastys and A. Sabelfeld. If this then what? controlling flows in iot apps. In CCS , page 1102–1119, 2018.
[7] S. Eberz S. Birnbach and I. Martinovic. Peeves: Physical event verification in smart homes. In CCS , page 1455–1467, 2019.
[8] O. Alrawi, C. Lever, M. Antonakakis, and F. Monrose. Sok: Security evaluation of home-based iot deployments. In IEEE S&P , pages 1362–1380, 2019.
[9] J. Jung E. Fernandes, A. Rahmati and A. Prakash. Decentralized action integrity for trigger-action iot platforms. In NDSS , 2018.
